summary:
PlotTwist is a free web app that helps farmers decide whether to change their crop rotation by turning NASA Earth data into plain-language advice and real dollar figures. A farmer traces their fields on satellite imagery, and PlotTwist builds a profile of each one. It draws on NASA weather, soil moisture, rainfall, and crop greenness data, plus USDA soil and crop history and USGS slope.

The Rotation Explorer scores three strategies: keeping the current rotation, adding a cover crop, or bringing in small grains. Each is rated on soil cover, crop diversity, pest pressure, and climate fit, and every reason is cited. The chosen strategy becomes an editable season-by-season plan. The finance tool compares that plan with the farmer's current rotation using published crop budgets, cost-share programs, and cash flow. It replays 40 years of real NASA weather at the farm to show how the plan holds up in drought and wet years.

Every value is labelled Measured, Estimated, or Check this info, and missing data is never filled with a guess. Field data stays in the farmer's browser. Built with Next.js and TypeScript and hosted on Vercel, PlotTwist aims to make soil-building practices less risky and easier to adopt.
details:
PlotTwist is a free web app that helps farmers decide whether to change their crop rotation and shows what the change would mean for their soil, workload, and finances. A farmer finds their farm by address, ZIP code, or map and traces each field on USGS satellite imagery. The app reads past crops from the USDA Cropland Data Layer, and the farmer confirms or corrects them. For each field, it automatically pulls public data: NASA POWER for weather, NASA SMAP for soil moisture, NASA GPM IMERG for rainfall, MODIS for vegetation, USDA SSURGO for soil, and USGS 3DEP for slope. Every value is labelled Measured, Estimated, or Check this info, with its source and date.

After a short questionnaire, the Rotation Explorer scores three strategies: keeping the current rotation, adding a cover crop, or bringing in small grains. Each is rated on soil cover, crop diversity, pest and disease pressure, and climate fit. The farmer can turn a strategy into an editable season-by-month plan. The Finance and Scenario Simulator then compares that plan with current practice, showing net return per acre, cash flow, break-even, cost-share programs like EQIP, and FSA microloans. It also replays 40 years of real NASA weather at that farm, so a farmer can see how a plan would have done in a bad year like 2012. Farmers can replace the defaults with their own numbers by importing invoices, yield files, and machine data, and they can export plans to PDF, spreadsheet, shapefile, and ISOXML.

PlotTwist makes NASA data usable without GIS skills, shows the cost and payback of a rotation change before the farmer commits, and labels every estimate honestly instead of guessing. It is free, needs no accounts or API keys, and keeps field data in the farmer’s browser. The goal is to help more farms adopt cover crops and diverse rotations, which improve soil health and cut erosion and runoff. It also gives small and beginning farmers tools that are usually limited to large operations, and it brings NASA Earth observation data into decisions made field by field.

The app is built with TypeScript, React, and Next.js, deployed on Vercel. It uses Leaflet and MapLibre for maps and is tested with Vitest and Playwright. The team developed it with VS Code, GitHub, and Claude Code as an AI coding assistant, and it runs in any modern browser on a laptop, tablet, or phone.

The project is creative in several ways. The 40-year weather replay works as a financial stress test that a farmer can feel. A color-swatch strip shows each field’s past, current, and planned crops at a glance. Farmer and Agronomist views show the same data in plain language or technical detail. Every number has a source, date, and confidence level, and the farmer’s own number always wins. The app can also read photographed invoices on the device.

The team weighed how much could realistically be built within the time available and focused on making the app easy for farmers to use. We also considered farmers’ finances, such as costs, cost-share programs, and cash flow, and designed the app so farmers can choose to share their data with one another, much like an open team. Finally, we wanted the data to be specific to each farmer’s own land rather than a local average, so every recommendation reflects the exact field it is made for.
